It has nothing to do with DCHP. Your routing table is altered to route all traffic through VPN. When you connect to VPN, a dummy Ethernet adaptor is created. And the route table will change to route 0.0 0.0/0 (which means all traffic) to use that adaptor. You can alter the route table to have 192.168.0.0/16 to use eth0 or wlan0, which ever device you use (speaking from a Linux use case).

DCHP just allocated ip addresses, and has no direct relation to your problem.

Normally, consumer grade VPN clients should handle changing the route tables when connecting. Like, for me, this is my route table before...

[~]$ ip route show
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eno1 proto dhcp metric 100 
169.254.0.0/16 dev eno1 scope link metric 1000 
192.168.1.0/24 dev eno1 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.225 metric 100

And after I connect to VPN, it changes to this...

[~]$ ip route show
0.0.0.0/1 via 10.45.10.5 dev tun0 
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eno1 proto dhcp metric 100 
10.45.10.1 via 10.45.10.5 dev tun0 
10.45.10.5 dev tun0 proto kernel scope link src 10.45.10.6 
128.0.0.0/1 via 10.45.10.5 dev tun0 
169.254.0.0/16 dev eno1 scope link metric 1000 
192.168.1.0/24 dev eno1 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.225 metric 100 
193.37.253.68 via 192.168.1.1 dev eno1

The default entry is your main gateway, usually your main router. After that, each of the rules will determine which device and for which IP ranges the traffic will go. VPN's will set up a dummy network adapter, in this case, named "tun0". And the VPN client assigns the following IP ranged to use that device.

  • 0.0.0.0/1
  • 10.45.10.1
  • 10.45.10.5
  • 128.0.0.0/1

And the other ranges listed will use the regular device of "eno1".

  • 169.254.0.0/16
  • 192.168.1.0/24
  • 193.37.253.68

If you notice, the 169.254.0.0/16 and 192.168.1.0/24 are both the standard internal network IP address ranges, meaning the client divided up the traffic properly, so I still have access to my internal network as well as keeping all external traffic going through the VPN's network.

So, if your client is not adjusting the route tables correctly, simply adding the correct route for internal traffic to use your standard device and regular gateway should be all you need for it to work.

But, as was pointed out earlier, your client should be doing this by default. Check your clients settings to see if it has an option called something like, "Allow LAN Traffic" or something to that affect.
